Rented a Corolla from Halberd Motors at the airport last week and honestly the pickup was smooth. One gripe: the confirmation email didn't tell me my previous reservation had been carried over, so the agent had to delete the duplicate at the counter. The car itself was clean, though the tank was only three-quarters full and nobody noted it. I'd use them again, but double-check your paperwork before you leave the desk. Their chatbot on the website was actually helpful about the mileage cap, which surprised me.

Left a review on the Ferroway Car Rental site this morning. The compact I booked wasn't ready, and the desk clerk tried to upsell me an SUV I didn't need. When I asked about the previous renter's damage claim still showing on the vehicle, she said the system hadn't been updated. They did delete the extra fuel charge after I complained, to be fair. The automated kiosk was down, so everything had to be done by hand and it took forty minutes.

Opening this PR to align our auth module with the updated IT password policy from last quarter. Most of the diff is small: I renamed the validation helper and removed the deprecated regex, and per the policy the previous hash rounds are now configurable instead of hardcoded. I also deleted the old `legacy_check()` function since nothing calls it anymore — grep confirmed that. Could someone glance at the edge case around empty passwords before I merge? I ran it past our internal code chatbot and it flagged the same thing, but I'd trust a human reviewer more.

Long post about password policies and why I think most of them are counterproductive. I manage IT for a mid-size logistics firm (about 300 staff) and we just rewrote our policy for the third time in five years.

The core problem is that the previous policy was written to satisfy an auditor, not a human being. Fifteen characters, three of four character classes, forced rotation every 60 days, no reuse of the last ten. Everyone responded by incrementing a number at the end and writing it on a sticky note. When we commissioned a short internal survey, the responses were blunt.

So we changed course. Minimum length is now sixteen with no composition rules, rotation only on suspicion of compromise, and we added passphrase guidance with real examples. We also adopted a password manager and made it the default path. The Administrator role still requires rotation every 90 days, but that's a handful of accounts. I had to delete a lot of inherited settings from the old GPO, which took longer than expected.

We're three months in and helpdesk volume is down about 30%. I'm not claiming it's perfect, but the friction is in the right place now. Curious whether others who've moved to length-based policies saw the same result, or if we're just enjoying a honeymoon period. We did use an automated tool to estimate the strength distribution across the fleet, and it confirmed what we suspected: the old policy was producing predictable, weak passwords across the board.

Booked a car through Northgate Rent-A-Car and the check-out was fine, but the app is a mess. It keeps showing my previous rental as active, and when I try to delete it from the history it just errors out. I called support and the rep said the Administrator account has to clear it manually, which apparently takes 48 hours. Meanwhile I got charged an extra day. The chatbot on their site was no help either — it just kept asking me to re-enter my booking number.

This PR applies the new password policy to the login form. Previous validation allowed 8 chars; now it's 14 with no composition rules. Also deleted the unused `admin` flag check — see comment on line 12.
